subject: Modern History
sub_topic: Anglo-French rivalry in India — Carnatic Wars

concepts.name: Background and Causes of Anglo-French Rivalry in India
key_dimensions: Extension of European dynastic and commercial rivalries (War of Austrian Succession, Seven Years' War) into Indian theatre
Competing trade interests of English East India Company vs French Compagnie des Indes Orientales
Strategic importance of Coromandel Coast, Carnatic region, and Deccan as the contested arena
Role of weak successor states post-Aurangzeb creating a power vacuum exploited by both powers

concepts.name: First Carnatic War (1746–1748): Context and Outcome
key_dimensions: Direct trigger: outbreak of War of Austrian Succession in Europe spilling into India
French capture of Madras (1746) under Dupleix after defeating British naval commander Peyton
Battle of St. Thome — French forces under Paradis defeated Nawab Anwaruddin's far larger army, demonstrating European military superiority over Indian forces
Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748): Madras returned to English in exchange for Louisbourg (Canada) — UPSC trap: outcome decided in Europe, not India

concepts.name: Dupleix's Political Strategy: Use of Indian Politics
key_dimensions: Pioneer of the policy of intervening in Indian succession disputes to extract territorial and financial concessions
Support for Chanda Sahib (Carnatic) and Muzaffar Jung (Hyderabad) against rival claimants backed by the English
Concept of 'subsidiary alliance' in embryonic form — French troops provided in exchange for territory/revenue
Why Dupleix's strategy ultimately failed: recall by French Company due to financial losses, lack of naval support, and Robert Clive's countermoves — a key comparative UPSC angle

concepts.name: Second Carnatic War (1749–1754): Succession Disputes as Battlefield
key_dimensions: Dual succession disputes: Carnatic (Chanda Sahib vs Anwaruddin/Muhammad Ali) and Hyderabad (Muzaffar Jung vs Nasir Jung)
French support for Chanda Sahib + Muzaffar Jung; English support for Muhammad Ali + Nasir Jung
Siege of Trichinopoly — the strategic pivot of the Second Carnatic War
Robert Clive's capture of Arcot (1751) and its defence: turned the tide psychologically and militarily in favour of the English — high-yield event

concepts.name: Siege of Arcot (1751): Military and Strategic Significance
key_dimensions: Clive captured Arcot (capital of Carnatic) with only 200 soldiers to divert Chanda Sahib's forces from Trichinopoly
Defended Arcot for 53 days against a force of 10,000 — inflection point establishing Clive's reputation
Strategic logic: indirect relief of Trichinopoly by threatening the enemy's political capital
UPSC trap: often confused as a 'battle' — it was primarily a siege and defence, not an open field engagement; also marks English transition from traders to political-military actors

concepts.name: Role of Indian Allies and Mercenary Commanders in the Carnatic Wars
key_dimensions: Marathas and Mysore as swing factors — both sides courted Maratha support (Morari Rao sided with English)
Chanda Sahib's dependence on French troops and his eventual capture and execution by Tanjore forces (1752)
Nawab of Hyderabad's court as a theatre of Franco-British proxy competition
Demonstrates that European success depended on building Indian coalitions, not purely military superiority

concepts.name: Recall of Dupleix (1754) and Its Consequences
key_dimensions: French Compagnie recalled Dupleix due to mounting costs, preferring trade over territorial ambition
Treaty of Pondicherry (1754): both sides agreed to non-interference in Indian politics — practically unenforceable
Structural weakness of French India: state-controlled company with less autonomy vs privately-driven English EIC
Dupleix's recall is a classic UPSC analytical question: French lost not on the battlefield but due to institutional/financial weaknesses

concepts.name: Third Carnatic War (1756–1763): Seven Years' War Extension
key_dimensions: Global context: Seven Years' War (1756–63) — Britain vs France across multiple continents simultaneously
Count de Lally's arrival (1758) to revive French fortunes — initial successes (capture of Fort St. David) followed by rapid decline
Battle of Wandiwash (1760) — decisive English victory under Sir Eyre Coote over French forces under Lally and Bussy
Fall of Pondicherry (1761): French stronghold razed to the ground by the English — symbolic end of French power in India

concepts.name: Battle of Wandiwash (1760): Decisive Engagement
key_dimensions: Fought on January 22, 1760 — English forces under Sir Eyre Coote defeated Lally's French army
Marquis de Bussy (France's most capable Indian commander) captured during the battle — removes key French asset
Military significance: ended French ability to wage offensive warfare in India
UPSC comparison trap: Wandiwash (ended French power) vs Plassey (1757, ended Nawab's power in Bengal) — both in same period but different theatres and implications

concepts.name: Treaty of Paris (1763): Final Settlement of Anglo-French Rivalry
key_dimensions: Ended Seven Years' War globally; France returned Pondicherry, Karikal, Mahe, Chandernagore, Yanam to English — then restored to France as trading posts only
Critical condition: France could not fortify these settlements or station troops — reduced to purely commercial entities
UPSC trap: France was NOT expelled from India entirely; it retained 5 enclaves but as de-militarised trading posts
Contrast with Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) — earlier treaty restored status quo; Treaty of Paris fundamentally altered the balance permanently

concepts.name: Marquis de Bussy and French Influence in Hyderabad
key_dimensions: Bussy stationed in Hyderabad (1751–1758) — wielded near-total influence over Nizam Salabat Jung, essentially controlling Deccan politics
Northern Circars (coastal Andhra territories) ceded to French — their only significant territorial holding in India
Bussy's recall by Lally to fight at Wandiwash: strategic blunder — weakened both fronts
Northern Circars later granted to English EIC by Nizam (1765 Diwani context) — French territorial legacy passed to British

concepts.name: Comparative Institutional Strengths: English EIC vs French Compagnie
key_dimensions: English EIC: joint-stock, privately owned, profit-driven, greater financial autonomy and reinvestment capacity
French Compagnie: state-controlled, dependent on royal treasury, financially constrained, less aggressive commercial expansion
English EIC had stronger naval support (Royal Navy superiority post-1757 globally)
UPSC analytical angle: institutional structure, not just battlefield outcomes, determined the long-term victor — often asked as 'Why did French fail in India?'

concepts.name: Naval Dimension of Anglo-French Rivalry in India
key_dimensions: Control of sea lanes critical for reinforcements and supply — English consistently superior at sea in Indian Ocean
French Admiral La Bourdonnais captured Madras (1746) but conflict with Dupleix over its fate weakened French position
Battle of Cuddalore (1758) — French naval victory under Comte de Lally, but strategically inconsequential
English naval dominance meant French land victories could never be consolidated — a structural asymmetry

concepts.name: Robert Clive: Rise to Prominence Through the Carnatic Wars
key_dimensions: Clive joined EIC as a clerk (writer), transitioned to military role during First Carnatic War
Arcot (1751) and subsequent engagements established him as the foremost English commander in India
Carnatic Wars as Clive's training ground before Bengal (Plassey, 1757) — UPSC often links these phases
Clive's methods: bold offensive action, psychological warfare, use of Indian allies — contrast with Dupleix's more political-diplomatic approach

concepts.name: Doctrine of 'Subsidiary Alliance': Embryonic Origins in Carnatic Wars
key_dimensions: Dupleix first practised providing European troops to Indian rulers in exchange for territory/revenue
English adopted and perfected this model — later systematised by Wellesley (1798 onwards)
Carnatic Wars demonstrate the template: back a claimant, win a battle, extract concessions
UPSC trap: Subsidiary Alliance formally attributed to Wellesley, but its conceptual origins trace to Dupleix's Carnatic strategy — a high-value analytical linkage

concepts.name: Significance of Carnatic as the Arena: Geographical and Political Factors
key_dimensions: Carnatic (roughly modern Tamil Nadu and coastal Andhra) — nominally under Mughal suzerainty via Hyderabad Nizam, practically autonomous
Arcot as capital of Carnatic Nawab — control of Arcot = political legitimacy in southern India
Proximity of Madras (English) and Pondicherry (French) bases — 160 km apart, making rivalry almost inevitable
Three-way power structure (Carnatic Nawab, Hyderabad Nizam, Maratha Confederacy) gave Europeans multiple intervention points

concepts.name: Outcome and Legacy of the Carnatic Wars: Establishment of British Supremacy
key_dimensions: French permanently neutralised as a political-military force in India after 1763
English EIC emerged as the dominant European power in South India, paving way for conquest of Bengal and beyond
Demonstrated that European powers could determine Indian succession disputes — a psychological shift in how Indian rulers perceived Europeans
Long-term legacy: Carnatic Wars as the 'laboratory' for British imperial methods (proxy wars, subsidised alliances, divide and rule) applied across India later

concepts.name: Count de Lally's Campaign and the Reasons for French Failure in the Third Carnatic War
key_dimensions: Lally's strategic errors: recalled Bussy from Hyderabad (weakening political influence), failed at Siege of Madras (1758–59)
Internal conflicts: Lally clashed with French councillors at Pondicherry, undermining administrative coherence
Inadequate naval support and supply disruptions due to English sea control
Lally later executed in France for 'betrayal' — controversial; highlights how French India suffered from poor civil-military coordination unlike the more cohesive English command structure

concepts.name: Impact of Carnatic Wars on Indian States: Nawabs, Nizams, and Marathas
key_dimensions: Carnatic Nawabs reduced to dependence on English after French elimination — Muhammad Ali became a pliant English ally
Nizam of Hyderabad lost French buffer, increasingly dependent on English — Northern Circars transferred to English (1765)
Marathas: their neutrality/opportunism during Carnatic Wars meant they missed the chance to prevent singular European dominance
Overall: Carnatic Wars marked the beginning of Indian rulers' subordination to European power — a structural transformation, not merely a series of battles
